title: The Wanderer and the Earth
hook: a king meets a young wanderer with nothing, and asks where his calm comes from
carry: the earth is a guru: pushed, it doesn't swerve
tomorrow: who is the path of action really for?

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma began with a goodbye: Uddhava asked to be taken along, and Krishna stayed to teach him instead.

A king out in the world meets a young man who owns nothing. No house, no plans, no worry on his face. The king is Yadu, an ancestor of Krishna's own clan, and he can't help asking. You're clever and capable, he says, yet you live like a child, untroubled. People all around are burning with wanting, and you stand there cool, like an elephant in a river while the forest burns. Where does your calm come from? Krishna tells this story to Uddhava early in their dialogue. The wanderer is an avadhuta, one who lives outside the world's usual rules. His answer: I've had many teachers. And the first one is right under your feet.
screen: `A KING MEETS A WANDERER.` → `WHERE DOES YOUR CALM COME FROM?` → `I'VE HAD MANY TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: The first teacher is the earth. In paraphrase, here's what the avadhuta learned from it: a steady person, even when pushed around by other beings, remembers that they too are moved by forces beyond their control, and doesn't step off the path. People dig the earth, plow it, build on it and walk on it all day. It doesn't shake anyone off. It keeps holding things up and growing food. This is karma from an unexpected side. Karma talk often starts with my actions and what comes back to me. The avadhuta turns it around. The other person, the one acting badly, is caught in a web of causes too. Not excused. Understood. Their action is theirs; my steadiness is mine. And the earth doesn't pretend nothing happened, or argue. It simply doesn't swerve. That isn't being a doormat. It's not letting someone else's bad day rewrite your path. After the earth come twenty-three more: the wind, the sky, water, fire, the moon, a python, a moth, a honeybee and others. Tradition identifies the wanderer with Dattatreya, and many Hindus know this list as his twenty-four gurus. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, a guru can be anything you learn from, and the world itself is a classroom. The list begins at the ground, with the teacher everybody stands on.
screen: `THE EARTH: PUSHED, AND STILL STEADY.` · `OTHERS ARE MOVED BY CAUSES TOO.` · `NOT A DOORMAT: JUST DON'T SWERVE.` · `TWENTY-FOUR GURUS.`

segments.voice: Feel what's holding you up, the chair, the floor, the earth under the building, and let your weight go into it. Bring to mind one person who pushed you lately with a sharp word or a careless move, and without replaying it, say to yourself: they were moved by things I can't see; then come back to the ground holding you. If you pray, you can hold that person before the One you pray to.
Karma. Action, and the web of causes behind it. From the earth the avadhuta learned that others are moved by causes too, and not to swerve.
Your line: the earth is a guru, pushed, it doesn't swerve. The ground takes every step and still holds. See you tomorrow.
